problems.title: Waves and efficiency
problems.statement: The GW-1 (16 SMs), one block per SM at a time.

problems.title: A big GPU, a medium GEMM
problems.statement: An H100 has 132 SMs. A 1024 × 1024 GEMM with 128 × 128 tiles, one tile per SM at a time.
problems.solution: 64 tiles on 132 SMs: 48% used. Smaller tiles, split-K or Stream-K are needed.

problems.title: Tile size versus tail
problems.statement: A 2048 × 2048 GEMM on a 108-SM GPU, one tile per SM at a time. Per-tile efficiency (from reuse): 128 × 128 tiles run at 90% of peak, 64 × 64 at 70%.

parts.prompt: With 64 × 64 (4 tiles per SM resident), in %?
Overall fraction of peak with 128 × 128, in %?

problems.solution: 128 × 128: 256 tiles, 3 waves, 79% → 71% overall. 64 × 64: 1,024 tiles, 3 waves of 432, 79% → 55%. The big tiles still win here, but by less than per-tile efficiency suggests; at other sizes the order flips. Libraries search.

problems.title: Split-K
problems.statement: A 512 × 512 × 8192 GEMM, 128 × 128 tiles, on the GW-1 (16 SMs, one block per SM).

parts.prompt: Extra traffic: partial results written and re-read, in MB (FP32), for split-K = 4?

hints: Each split writes a full partial C tile.
problems.solution: (a) 16, exactly one wave: fine here. On a 108-SM GPU, 16 tiles would use 15%; split-K = 4 gives 64 blocks. (c) Each of the 4 splits writes a 512 × 512 partial (1 MB) that a reduction re-reads: 8.4 MB extra, small next to the 33.5 MB of A and B ($2 \times 512 \times 8192 \times 4$ bytes) the GEMM reads anyway.

problems.title: Uneven blocks
problems.statement: Row i of a triangular computation costs i + 1 units, for i = 0..n−1 with n = 64. One block per row, 16 SMs, blocks dispatched in row order to the least-loaded SM.
problems.solution: (a) 2,080 units; (b) ideal 130 per SM. In-order dispatch puts the heaviest rows last; pairing row i with row 63 − i (every pair costs 65) or dispatching heaviest first gets close to 130.

problems.title: Simulating the dispatcher
problems.statement: Same triangular work: rows dispatched in order 0, 1, …, 63 to the least-loaded SM (ties to the lowest index).
hints: Greedy list scheduling; simulate it (Part 0's scheduler drill).
problems.solution: (a) 160, (b) 130 (ideal 130), (c) 0.812. Longest-processing-time-first is a classic 4/3-approximation for this scheduling problem; on GPUs it means launching heavy blocks first.

problems.title: Persistent blocks
problems.statement: A persistent kernel launches exactly one block per resident slot and loops over tiles from an atomic counter.

options: No per-block launch/setup cost per tile
Control over tile order (e.g. heavy first, L2-friendly)
Automatic perfect balance with tiles of different sizes
Easy fusion of an epilogue across tiles

hints: The tail of the last tiles still exists.
problems.solution: Persistence removes per-tile scheduling cost and gives you the schedule, but uneven tiles still leave a tail unless tiles are fine-grained or split (Stream-K).

problems.title: Stream-K's share
problems.statement: A GEMM with 25 tiles of 64 k-iterations each on 16 SMs. Stream-K gives every SM an equal share of all k-iterations.

parts.prompt: Tiles split between two SMs (at most)?

hints: SM boundaries fall every 100 iterations; tile boundaries every 64.
problems.solution: 1,600 iterations, 100 per SM. Boundaries at multiples of 100 that aren't multiples of 64 split a tile: 15 internal boundaries, and none of 100, 200, …, 1500 is a multiple of 64 except 1,600 itself, so up to 15 tiles need a fix-up (partial sums combined). Balance is perfect at the cost of those fix-ups.

problems.title: Other work on the GPU
problems.statement: Your kernel runs while another process occupies 4 of the GW-1's 16 SMs.
problems.solution: ⌈48/12⌉ = 4 waves instead of 3: a 33% slowdown with no change to your code. Benchmarks on shared machines measure the neighbours too.

problems.title: Choosing blocks for a reduction
problems.statement: A grid-stride kernel on the GW-1 (16 SMs, 8 blocks of 256 resident per SM), with each block doing equal work.

parts.prompt: Blocks for exactly one full wave?
With a grid-stride loop, is 129 blocks a problem?
options: Yes: the 129th block runs alone as a second wave, unless each block's work shrinks to match

hints: Equal work per block means the extra block takes a full block-time.
problems.solution: 128 blocks fill one wave. 129 blocks with equal shares make a second wave of one block: about 50% efficiency. Size grid-stride grids to the machine (multiples of the resident count).
